newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Alberta projects fourth straight surplus.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Alberta projects fourth straight surplus.

text.p: The Canadian province of Alberta, on the eve of an expected election call, delivered its 1997/98 budget on Tuesday projecting a surplus of C$144 million.
However, Alberta Treasurer Jim Dinning said the surplus could grow to over C$800 million if crude oil and natural gas prices stay above forecast levels.

Alberta assumed in the budget that the West Texas Intermediate oil price would average US$19 per barrel and wellhead natural gas price would average C$1.55 per thousand cubic feet. It also assumed a Canadian dollar valued at US$0.75.

As predicted, Canada's petroleum-rich province recorded a 1996/97 surplus of at least C$2.23 billion, Dinning said. That was up from a forecast made in last year's budget speech of C$23 million to C$568 million.
Tuesday's projected surplus would be Alberta's fourth consecutive positive financial statement.

Ralph Klein, Alberta's popular Conservative premier, was widely expected to call a provincial election as early as Tuesday evening. That would mean a new budget would be introduced during the new legislative session that would begin after a provincial vote.
But Dinning, who has served notice he would not seek re-election after four years as treasurer, said Tuesday's budget would be re-introduced without major changes after the expected spring election.
The new budget projected total provincial revenues at C$14.7 billion and government spending at C$13.9 billion.
The 1.2 percent jump in government spending would be Alberta's first increase since 1993/94.

Spending on health care, the Klein government's most sensitive political issue after years of cuts, was projected to increase by C$128 million. Education spending was slated to rise by C$91 million and expenditures on senior citizen programs by C$180 million.
Under Alberta legislation, all the 1996/97 surplus will go to reduction of the province's net debt, which currently stands at C$3.5 billiion, exluding pension liabilities.
